# Talking Points — Engineering Harnesses & Guardrails
_For: presenting to Accenture's Innovation Lead (Managing Director)_
_Pair with: `zimmermann-pwa-guardrails-tree.md` — same 12 sections, same order, so you can move through both side by side._

---

## Opening — set the frame

> "You asked what engineering harnesses and guardrails we have in place on this build, so I want to
> walk you through where things actually stand — this is what we've put together so far, not a finished
> system. I'll go through it in the same order as the diagram I've shared, roughly following how a change
> moves from a developer's — or an AI agent's — hands into production. Some of this is solid, some of it
> we're still hardening, and I'd rather be upfront about both."

---

## The walkthrough (12 points, same order as the diagram)

**§1 — Branch & Merge Guardrails**
> "Feature work happens on its own branch, never straight on the branch that goes live. The closer a
> branch is to production, the more sign-off it needs to merge."

**§2 — File Protection Tiers**
> "Files are grouped roughly by how much damage a mistake could do — a homepage tweak is treated
> differently to a change touching payments or design tokens. The higher tiers need a named approver.
> It's not a perfect system, but it's meant to take 'did anyone notice this was sensitive' out of memory."

**§3 — CI/CD Pipeline**
> "Before a person reviews a change, it's already run through automated tests, an accessibility check,
> and a performance budget. Worth flagging: one of those checks — a contract test with a partner API —
> is still a placeholder today, so I don't want to overstate that one."

**§4 — AI PR Review Tooling**
> "An AI review tool also looks at every pull request, checking for a handful of specific things like
> exposed secrets or unsafe HTML. It's an extra pair of eyes, not a replacement for the human review that
> still happens after it."

**§5 — Git Hooks**
> "Before a commit even leaves someone's laptop, it's checked for things like accidentally-committed
> secrets and commit message formatting. Small and unglamorous, but it catches mistakes early and cheaply."

**§6 — Claude Code Session Harness**
> "We're using Claude Code, an AI coding agent, on parts of this build. It's mechanically prevented from
> writing to production branches, not just told not to, and it inherits the same file-ownership tiers a
> person would. This is newer territory for us, and we're still learning where the edges of it are."

**§7 — TypeScript / Lint / Build Enforcement**
> "Type checking and lint rules catch a class of mistakes before code even runs. Not everything here is
> a hard block yet — some of it is still a warning rather than something that stops a merge."

**§8 — Test Harness**
> "Unit tests, component-level tests, and end-to-end browser tests each cover a different layer, so we're
> not leaning on one kind of test to catch everything."

**§9 — Environment, Secrets & Deployment Gates**
> "Credentials are scoped by environment, and promoting to each environment needs the right person's
> sign-off. Nothing clever here — just trying to keep it boring and consistent."

**§10 — Contentful Sync Safety**
> "Our content syncing only ever adds fields, never removes them, so a bad push can't silently delete
> something that's live."

**§11 — AI-Assisted QA Six-Stage Pipeline**
> "Separately, there's a QA process where AI helps draft acceptance criteria and test cases — but a
> person signs off at three separate points before any of it goes further. This one lives more in our
> process documentation than in the codebase itself, so I'd treat it as a work-in-progress alongside
> everything else."

**§12 — Security & Privacy Boundaries**
> "Third-party scripts wait for a customer's consent before loading, and we've tried to limit how much
> damage one integration failing could do to the rest of the site. Also mostly a documentation-level
> guardrail — we didn't re-verify every part of the implementation for this walkthrough."

---

## Closing — the takeaway

> "So that's roughly where we are, section by section: explicit rather than assumed ownership, some
> automated checks ahead of human review, an attempt to constrain the AI agent the same way we'd
> constrain a person, and a human decision point that doesn't get skipped. It's not complete, and I'd
> rather tell you what's still rough than gloss over it. If parts of this turn out useful beyond this
> account, that'd be a nice outcome, but it's early to claim that — right now it's just what we've built
> for this one."

---

## Q&A soundbites (if pushed on specifics)

- **"What stops the AI from just breaking something in production?"**
  → "It can't write to a production branch — that's a mechanical block, not just an instruction. I
  wouldn't call it bulletproof, but it's a real constraint, not a policy on paper."

- **"Is this mature, or held together with tape?"**
  → "Somewhere in between. We reviewed it ourselves and found a couple of gaps — one CI check is a
  placeholder, one approval step is enforced by process rather than code. We'd rather surface that
  ourselves than have it found later."

- **"Does this slow the team down?"**
  → "Some overhead, but a lot of it replaces manual review time rather than adding to it. I don't have
  hard numbers on the net effect yet."

- **"Could we reuse this on another account?"**
  → "Possibly, in shape if not in specifics — but we haven't tried transplanting it anywhere else, so
  I'd treat that as a hope rather than a proven claim."

I'll structure this as: yes, the frontend code is inspectable (unavoidable for SPAs), but what matters is that secrets and business logic enforcement aren't exposed, which I can confirm from the credential boundary table. The actual commerce operations — pricing, inventory, payments, order creation — all happen server-side through SFCC and Adyen APIs regardless of what's visible in the frontend code.

For the SSR/CSR split, product pages are server-rendered for SEO while cart and checkout use an SSR shell with client-side data loading because personalized and authenticated data shouldn't be rendered server-side where it could leak across requests. content.text:
Short answer: yes, but that's true of any browser-rendered app, not a Zimmermann-specific gap — and the guardrails are built around that reality rather than pretending otherwise.

**What's inherently visible:** This is a React-based PWA (SSR + client-side hydration), so any JavaScript that runs in the browser — component logic, rendering code, API-calling code — is downloadable and inspectable by anyone via view-source or dev tools. Minification/bundling makes it harder to read, not impossible. There's no way to truly hide client-side code in a browser, and that's not something these guardrails try to solve.

**What's actually protected (§12 / TSD §4.1's credential boundary table):** The line isn't drawn at "code visibility," it's drawn at *credentials*. MRT-mediated secrets — MuleSoft, Contentful Preview/Management tokens, the Google Maps API key, the reCAPTCHA secret key — never reach the browser bundle at all; those calls happen server-side. What *is* browser-direct is only stuff that's public by design: the SLAS client ID, Adyen's client key, Narvar's account ID, the GTM container ID, Didomi's notice ID, reCAPTCHA's site key — all meant to be visible, none of them usable to do anything on their own.

**Why exposed frontend logic isn't the real risk here:** Pricing, inventory, payment authorization, and order creation are all re-validated server-side through SFCC SCAPI / MRT / Adyen's server API — the frontend just displays and requests. Someone reading the bundle could see *how* the UI calls those APIs, but couldn't forge a price or a payment, because the server doesn't trust the client's math.

**One thing I haven't verified:** whether production builds strip source maps (that affects how easy the bundle is to read, though it's not a security boundary either way). If that's likely to come up as a follow-up, I can dig into the build config and confirm — want me to check?

Not as a single named thing — no `.claude/skills/nfr-*` and no unified "NFR sign-off gate" like the three human gates in §11. But coverage of the major NFR categories is real, it's just distributed across the 12 sections rather than consolidated under one banner. Breaking it down:

**Reliability / availability** — AGENTS.md has an explicit graceful-degradation policy (each integration must fail independently, no silent fallback to a different checkout flow), and production rollout requires an AU canary at <0.5% error rate over 2h before wider release (§9).

I should explain that headless architecture decouples the frontend presentation layer from the backend commerce engine—in this case, SFCC handles all the commerce logic (products, pricing, cart, checkout, orders) and exposes it through APIs like SCAPI, while the PWA Kit React app in this repo is the separate frontend that consumes those APIs. content.text:
"Headless" means the commerce backend (the system that owns product catalog, pricing, cart, checkout, promotions, order management) is completely decoupled from the presentation layer (the actual website UI) — they're separate applications talking over an API, instead of one monolithic app where the backend renders its own pages.

**In this project specifically:**
- **The "head" that's been cut off:** Salesforce Commerce Cloud's own storefront rendering (the traditional SFCC/Demandware storefront templates). SFCC still runs, but purely as a commerce engine — catalog, pricing, cart, checkout, order management.
- **What talks to it:** this repo (`zimmermann-pwa`), a separate React app (Salesforce's PWA Kit) that calls SFCC's Shopper Commerce API (SCAPI) over HTTP, gets JSON back, and renders the actual pages itself.
- **Where it runs:** on Salesforce Managed Runtime (MRT), Salesforce's own hosting for PWA Kit apps — not inside SFCC itself.

**Why this matters for the "is code exposed" question from earlier:** headless is exactly why that answer holds up. The frontend app — the thing whose JavaScript is downloadable in a browser — is a thin presentation layer with no direct access to SFCC's database, admin capabilities, or internal business logic. It only ever gets what SCAPI chooses to return over the API. Someone reading the frontend bundle sees *how we call and render* commerce data — they don't get anywhere near the commerce engine itself, which never ships any code to the browser at all.

**The tradeoff, in plain terms:** headless buys flexibility (one commerce backend, potentially multiple frontends/storefronts) at the cost of complexity — you now own the frontend app, its hosting, its build pipeline, and its own security surface (which is most of what the 12 guardrail sections are actually about), instead of getting all of that bundled into the commerce platform for free.
